title: Did we overpay for a unit in Sunway, and how do we keep buying more?
excerpt: A couple nearing 50 paid RM1,250 per sq ft for a student-let unit in Bandar Sunway. Sean says judge price against today's market and rent, not the first buyer's price, and explains how rent helps you borrow again.

question.asker: From Mr T, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Mr T runs the family eatery in his hometown and is nearly 50. He and his wife own a bungalow bought for RM717,000 in 2011, with about RM300,000 left on a flexi loan with an overdraft facility, plus an inherited shop lot and old house. After spending heavily on renovation and their three children's international education, they have about RM400,000 to RM500,000 saved. His wife has just bought a 460 sq ft unit in Bandar Sunway at about RM1,250 per sq ft, let to students at about RM2,700 a month; the previous owner paid RM517,000 in 2017.
question.text: Was the price too high, is there room for growth, should he use the overdraft to buy more, and how does anyone keep buying property after property?

answer.quote: I do not look at what was the purchase price of the previous buyer.
answer.summary: Judge the price against today's market and the rent, not against what the first owner paid. With a normal 90% loan the rent would roughly cover the instalment, so it isn't a bad buy, and in a fully built-up area growth will come from rising rents rather than new projects. To keep buying, let rent count as income for the next loan.

reasons.title: Compare with today, not 2017
reasons.body: Few people would have bought back then anyway. Check the price per square foot of similar units nearby and the yield: a 90% loan of about RM513,000 over 35 years at 4% costs about RM2,600 a month, against a tenancy of about RM2,700.

reasons.title: Mature areas grow through rent
reasons.body: With trains, universities and malls already in place, new infrastructure won't add much. But as student demand pushes rents up, investors will pay more for a unit whose rent covers their instalment, and that becomes the exit.

reasons.title: Rent can help you borrow again
reasons.body: Banks count rent shown by a tenancy agreement, six months of bank statements and the SPA, usually at 80% and at some banks 100%. On a RM5,000 salary, a RM1,500 instalment with RM1,700 rent leaves more borrowing power than before the purchase.

reasons.title: An overdraft is like refinancing
reasons.body: Drawing on the flexi loan's overdraft costs much the same as refinancing the bungalow. With the children moving out, downsizing from a 6,300 sq ft bungalow would free more cash than either.

actions: Check recent prices per square foot and rents for similar units around Bandar Sunway to judge what you paid.
Buy units where the rent covers the instalment, so each one adds to your borrowing power for the next.
Keep tenancy agreements and six months of rent records ready for your next loan application.
Look for below-market prices at auctions or through bulk purchases; a subsale is usually at market price.
Spend on renovation only what keeps a home practical, since heavy renovation adds little at resale.
caveat: Sean doesn't treat transit-oriented development as essential: developers already price it in, and units without a train link can still yield well. He couldn't comment on a new project's value before its prices were known.
sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #227. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer and Sean stated them in October 2023. Sean says he is a client, not the owner, of FAR Capital, a bulk purchase club he suggests in this episode.
